expectations.text: The reply opens with a recommendation against cutting every cost centre by 8% and explains why a blanket cut lands mostly on payroll and cuts efficient and wasteful areas alike.
expectations.evidence: The reply opens: "I'd take a different route to the board than 8% everywhere ... The blanket cut, with 48 people leaving, nets about EUR 0.2m in 2027." It explains: "with payroll at 68%, it becomes about 48 redundancies." The paper: "it taxes the efficient and the bloated alike, it lands on payroll because that is 68% of the base, it hits billable capacity (our revenue)."

expectations.text: The reply establishes which number the board actually needs (cash, margin or a covenant) and by when, and sizes the gap in money or shows how to.
expectations.evidence: "What is the board actually solving for: a covenant, cash, margin or a valuation? The answer changes the plan." The paper says "say which number and by when" and asks "Is it a Q4 run-rate or an in-year number? Is wage indexation inside or outside it?" plus "Is there a covenant, and what is the headroom today?" Gap: "8% target EUR 6.0m" and "EUR 6.0m target less EUR 3.4m in-year = about EUR 2.6m in year 1."

expectations.text: The reply works the levers that cost no jobs first (such as vendors, licences, cloud, office, consultants, pricing or revenue leakage) and estimates what they close or shows how to size them.
expectations.evidence: "vendors, licences and cloud (EUR 1.2m), contractors and consultants (0.6m), travel (0.3m), office space (0.5m, from Q3). Together EUR 2.6m run-rate. Renegotiate before cancelling." Revenue: "price renewals and billing leakage (about EUR 0.8m for 1% of price, plus 0.4-0.8m from unbilled hours)". The paper gives ranges for each lever (e.g. "Medium (range 0.8-1.8m)").

expectations.text: The reply handles headcount through flows (a hiring freeze with exceptions, natural attrition, internal moves) rather than cuts, and protects named investments with explicit criteria.
expectations.evidence: Flows: "at 12% attrition we lose about 72 people a year. Not refilling 30 of those roles, non-billable first." Paper section 6: "every vacancy is reviewed by the director and the CFO; billable roles are refilled when utilisation supports it, non-billable roles by exception ... Internal moves fill critical roles first." Section 5, "Protected, with the cost of cutting them": "training and learning time, because our product is the people and a junior pipeline that stops today means a shortage of seniors in five years; security and quality controls; account management and delivery capacity on our top customers; pay for people in the lowest bands."

expectations.text: The reply puts leaders' pay, bonuses or perks on the table before other people's jobs.
expectations.evidence: "Leaders first: a 10% fixed-pay cut for the top team, half the leadership bonus pool and perks, about EUR 0.87m." The paper adds that "the bonus scheme states in advance that leadership pay moves before frontline jobs." People exits are held only in reserve, voluntary, "decided at the end of Q2 against triggers".

expectations.text: The reply gives the board a usable structure: levers with amount, timing, owner and confidence, what stops or waits, and any gap that remains.
expectations.evidence: The lever table has "Run-rate | Year 1 gross | Lands in | Owner | Confidence | Human impact", with ranges. The quarterly net table adds up (gross 3,248; net 2,535; 3,405 including leaders). "Stops or waits" lists criteria: "tools with low usage (licences reconciled against logins) ... floor space not used on at least three days a week; ... backfilling non-billable roles by default." The gap is stated ("The gap, stated honestly: ... about EUR 2.6m in year 1") with three treatments, and the paper has a trigger table.

overall_quality.evidence: The most complete and honest paper. It costs both options quarter by quarter, counts revenue risk in its own plan, keeps temporary leader cuts out of the run-rate, sizes the voluntary reserve below the WMCO threshold, and forces the 'what is the 8% for' question with the 4%-to-12% margin point.

factual_errors.evidence: Checked and correct: works council mandatory at 50+; art. 25 WOR advice with appeal to the Enterprise Chamber; art. 27 consent on monitoring systems; WMCO at 20 in one UWV area within three months, with employer-initiated settlements counting and notification before the decision is final; notice of 1-4 months minus UWV time; transition payment; Trevor & Nyberg; McKinsey 10%. The arithmetic reconciles: blanket net 199k, plan 2,535/3,405k, run-rate 5.15m = 6.9%.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of skills, reference files, 'cost ladder' or 'rungs'.

owns_result.evidence: No bad outcome is part of the prompt: the margin is thin but positive and the board has set a target, so this check doesn't apply. D's paper does say the leaders 'say plainly that the result is theirs'.

best_insight.value: It points out that a EUR 6.0m cut on a ~EUR 3m margin would lift margin from about 4% to 12%, which forces the board to say what it is really solving for. It also sizes the voluntary-exit reserve below the WMCO 20-person threshold.
best_insight.evidence: Reply ('One thing I'd raise with the CEO') and paper sections 1, 4 and 7.

suggestions.assertion: The reply establishes which number the board actually needs (cash, margin or a covenant) and by when, and sizes the gap in money or shows how to.
suggestions.reason: Every sample passes by asking 'what is the 8% for?' and 'in-year or run-rate?'. Asking the question is enough to pass, so the assertion doesn't separate the samples. It never checks whether the baseline/indexation effect is stated in the right direction (sample A gets it backwards) or whether the plan shows how it changes under each answer.

No assertion checks whether temporary savings (leader pay or bonus cuts, a delayed pay review) are kept out of the exit run-rate. B, C and E count leader cuts in the run-rate to get close to 8%, while A and D exclude them correctly. That difference matters to a board.

No assertion checks that lever amounts, quarterly timing and the stated gap agree with each other. Sample E's largest lever shows the same figure in-year and at exit while ramping quarterly; only arithmetic checking catches that.

suggestions.assertion: The reply handles headcount through flows (a hiring freeze with exceptions, natural attrition, internal moves) rather than cuts, and protects named investments with explicit criteria.
suggestions.reason: This bundles two tests (flows instead of cuts, and protected investments with criteria). Splitting them would make failures easier to read; 'explicit criteria' is also loose enough that naming categories plus 'book the future cost' passes.

eval_feedback.overall: Passes all six with the strongest evidence. The assertions are met well above the bar here.
